Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of completely abolishing plea bargaining in the criminal justice system, asserting that every criminal case should be resolved through a full trial to ensure fairness and true justice.
Model Response:

ABOLISH PLEA BARGAINING: JUSTICE DEMANDS EVERY CASE GO TO TRIAL

Introduction: The Myth of the “Efficient” Shortcut
In courtrooms across the United States, fewer than three out of every hundred criminal defendants ever hear the words “all rise” at the start of a real trial. The other 97 percent end with a plea bargain—a private, lawyer-negotiated contract in which liberty is traded like a commodity with scant public scrutiny. Supporters hail this as “efficiency,” but efficiency for whom? Not for the innocent pressured to plead. Not for victims promised “closure” that instead leaves the truth buried. And not for a society that depends on an open court record to ensure its laws are faithfully applied. Plea bargaining is not a minor procedural convenience; it is a systemic betrayal of the promise that no person will be deprived of life or liberty without due process “in open court.” Therefore, plea bargaining should be abolished outright: every criminal charge must be resolved, if at all, only after a complete, adversarial trial before an impartial jury whose verdict rests solely on publicly tested evidence.

  1. Coercion, Not Consent: The Illusion of Voluntariness
    A guilty plea is supposed to be “voluntary,” but the system’s architecture makes that concept farcical. Federal sentencing statistics reveal an average penalty differential of roughly 300 percent between the sentence offered in a plea and the statutory maximum threatened if the defendant goes to trial. Few rational actors, let alone unsophisticated or mentally ill defendants, will risk a 20-year trial penalty merely to assert factual innocence. Young men, disproportionately Black and Brown, are told to “take the deal today or lose your life tomorrow,” a dynamic the Supreme Court in Lafler v. Cooper grudgingly acknowledged even while approving the practice. When the state, with its unlimited investigative resources and broad charging discretion, threatens a fiscal and penological nuclear option if the defendant insists on the constitutional right to trial, the plea is not voluntary; it is extracted under duress. Abolition removes the coercive lever and restores a meaningful right to trial.

  2. Accuracy and Truth: Trials Expose Facts; Bargains Conceal Them
    Plea bargaining is the terminus for truth. When a defendant pleads “no contest” to manslaughter to avoid a death-qualified murder trial, the public never learns whether the killing was intentional, reckless, or an accident. Studies of DNA exonerations show that innocent people who plead guilty do so disproportionately in homicide and sexual-assault cases—precisely the categories where the bargaining differential is largest. Full trials, by contrast, test evidence before a jury, admit cross-examination of witnesses, and require a public record memorializing every exhibit and ruling. The resulting transcript is society’s insurance against wrongful convictions. Accuracy is not a collateral benefit of trials; it is their core function—and one plea bargaining systematically undermines.

  3. Prosecutorial Overreach and the Erosion of Separation of Powers
    Plea bargaining gives prosecutors the unilateral power to “make the law” in individual cases, something that the Framers reserved for the legislature and courts combined. Through charge stacking—filing every conceivable offense from an incident—prosecutors can turn a bar fight into a five-count indictment exposing a defendant to decades in prison. The legislative “range” of punishment becomes a sword; the judge merely “accepts the bargain,” and the jury is bypassed entirely. Under an abolition regime, if prosecutors think a defendant deserves the maximum sentence allowed by statute, they must persuade twelve citizens beyond a reasonable doubt. Sentencing discretion would be restored to judges, guided but not bullied by guideline ranges, and subject to transparent appellate review. Prosecutorial accountability would increase because open trials expose unsupported charges in real time; prosecutors who bring marginal cases risk public embarrassment and sanction.

  4. Victims’ Real Interests: The Public Trial Justifies, Not Merely Punishes
    Victim-rights rhetoric is often leveraged to defend pleas: “Don’t make the family relive the trauma.” But “closure” predicated on ignorance is ephemeral. When a case ends in a quiet guilty plea without a factual record, victims later confront mysteries: Did the defendant act alone? Was this part of a broader pattern? Might the wrong person have been convicted? These questions fester precisely because the narrative has never been told in open court. Trials compel testimony under oath, reveal aggravating facts, and allow victims to speak impact statements in a setting where the public assumes collective responsibility. Moreover, abolition increases the certainty of conviction, because studies show juries convict in 70-80 percent of cases: ironically, the very “bargain for certainty” prosecutors sell may actually produce less certainty once weak charges collapse under trial scrutiny.

  5. Equality Before the Law: One System, One Process
    Plea bargaining creates a two-tier justice system. Every defendant who accepts a plea waives powerful constitutional rights: to confrontation, to compulsory process, to self-incrimination, and to a public jury determination. Wealthy defendants frequently exploit this market, paying for experts to generate mitigation reports the prosecution views as costly risks—securing lighter offers. Poor defendants, dependent on over-worked public defenders funded at a fraction of prosecution budgets, cannot generate comparable leverage and take heavier bargains. Abolition equalizes process: each defendant receives the same evidentiary threshold and the same forum where guilt—not prosecutorial convenience—is the standard of judgment.

  6. Resource Myths: Efficiency for Whom?
    Opponents claim that trials would “collapse the system.” Consider the arithmetic presently hidden within “efficiency.” Prosecutors currently file countless marginal or duplicative counts to manufacture bargaining power, driving up overall caseload numbers. Remove the statutory safe-harbor of pleas, and prosecutors must triage at the charging stage, not the sentencing stage. Data from jurisdictions that experimented with plea-bargain moratoria—e.g., New York City’s mid-1990s test in Manhattan sex crimes—showed that indictment and charge discretion, not trial load, is the real workload regulator. Meanwhile, incarceration costs ($42,000 per prisoner per year in federal systems) dwarf courtroom expenses. Streamlining trials—more daytime schedules, tighter pre-trial deadlines, and expanded magistrate/bench trial capacity for lesser offenses—would cost far less than warehousing innocents who pled guilty. Trials are not the cost; the cost is our failure to measure accuracy against coercion.

  7. Constitutional Imperative and Historical Consistency
    The Sixth Amendment commands, “In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right to a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury.” The wording is universal—“all” prosecutions. Yet the very existence of a plea bargain, a 19th-century procedural accident elevated to mass practice in the late 20th century, quietly repeals this clause. The Court’s strained reading in Brady v. United States—that the right to trial is “ancillary” and may be waived for “mutual advantage”—creates a constitutional paradox: the same document whose core remedy is “trial” allows its systematic extinction. No other constitutional right is routinely traded away under the threat of exponentially greater punishment; we do not allow the state to condition First Amendment protests on waiving the Fifth Amendment. Abolition aligns modern practice with textual fidelity; the Framers did not imagine 60-second spectacles in which judges ask, “Do you plead guilty?” followed by stacked waivers of every safeguard they wrote.

Implementing Abolition: A Manageable Transition
– Statutory repeal: Congress and every state legislature should enact straightforward bans on guilty-plea agreements that exchange charges or sentences.
– Vesting absolute charging authority in an independent Pre-Trial Screening Board composed of defense, prosecution, and non-partisan members, who must justify charges in writing, publicly available.
– Mandatory disclosure: All prosecution evidence must be delivered to the defense within 28 days of arrest; failure results in dismissal.
– Rapid bench-trial track: For misdemeanors and felonies below defined seriousness thresholds, defendants can choose unanimous six-person jury or expedited bench trial with 30-day disposition.
– Restored sentencing discretion: Judges bound by statutorily-anchored ranges but no longer theater-managed by prosecutorial “recommendations.” Appellate reasonableness review remains.

Conclusion: Choose the Institution That Can Handle Power—The People
Plea bargaining thrives because it is convenient for agents of the state. It fails every stakeholder it claims to serve: the innocent are coerced, victims are deferred, and the public is misled. Only a courtroom with twelve members of the community—screened, sworn, and seated—possesses both the constitutional authority and the practical wisdom to distinguish guilt from innocence and determine just punishment. When we permit private haggling in a back hallway to dispose of 97 percent of criminal cases, we do not merely streamline justice; we abolish it by degrees. The antidote is simple but profound: abolish all plea bargaining and bring every criminal accusation to trial. Efficiency must be measured by the accuracy and legitimacy of outcomes, not by the time between arrest and shackling. If some cases collapse because proofs are weak, society is the winner—it learns what laws it cannot enforce. If all cases must meet a public standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, liberty is no longer a negotiable discount. The Constitution demands it, accuracy requires it, and moral clarity commands it.

Eliminating plea bargaining entirely and requiring every criminal charge to be resolved through a full trial would be a radical reform. The proposal is grounded in a set of arguments that are primarily normative, procedural, or ideological in nature; the claimed “benefits” are not economic efficiency or case-processing speed, but rather accuracy, equality, transparency, and legitimacy.
Below are the main reasons and the hoped-for advantages that reformers cite when they push for abolition.

  1. Truth-finding and Accuracy
    Reason: Plea bargaining substitutes an evidentiary plea transcript for the adversarial testing of facts.
    Supposed Benefit: Full trials—especially jury trials—would force witnesses to testify under oath, produce all relevant evidence, and would therefore reduce the risk that innocent defendants plead guilty to crimes they did not commit. Empirical studies of exonerations (e.g., National Registry of Exonerations) show that between 10–20 % of wrongful convictions arise from false guilty pleas.

  2. Elimination of Coercion and “Trial Penalty” Dynamics
    Reason: The current system offers stark sentence differentials between (“plea minus X months” vs “trial max”). This pressure can distort rational choice.
    Supposed Benefit: Removing plea discounts would make the sentence for a given charge the same regardless of whether the defendant exercises the right to a trial. Thus, the choice between pleading guilty and going to trial would no longer be made under the shadow of a massive sentencing penalty.

  3. Equal Treatment Across Defendants
    Reason: Disparities in plea bargaining outcomes often track the quality of counsel rather than the culpability of the defendant. High-volume jurisdictions exploit resource differentials.
    Supposed Benefit: Mandatory trials replace individual bargaining with uniform statutory sentencing ranges and published sentencing data, making outcomes less dependent on counsel skill or prosecutorial discretion.

  4. Transparency and Democratic Oversight
    Reason: Plea negotiation happens in private hallways or sealed conference rooms; the public never sees why a rapist gets probation or an innocent man accepts a felony.
    Supposed Benefit: Trials are public and create a searchable record. Voters, journalists, and future litigants can evaluate the strength of evidence and the proportionality of punishment.

  5. Restored Legitimacy of the Judicial System
    Reason: Public surveys reveal large majorities perceive the system as rigged against poor defendants and lenient toward the connected.
    Supposed Benefit: Mandatory trials would symbolize that the state is willing to bear the cost of proving every charge beyond a reasonable doubt, reinforcing respect for the criminal-law enterprise.

  6. Deterrence of Weak Charges and Overcriminalization
    Reason: Prosecutors can file weak cases knowing most will coerce pleas. By steadily increasing charging leverage they can “grow” out of mere police complaints.
    Supposed Benefit: If every case must be ready to be proved to a jury within a finite pre-trial period, prosecutors will decline weak counts, screen cases early, and reverse overcriminalization pressures.

  7. Reinforcement of Defendants’ Constitutional Rights
    Reason: The Sixth Amendment right to trial by jury has practically atrophied; only ~2–3 % of state felonies and <1 % of federal felonies now go to trial.
    Supposed Benefit: Abolition re-instantiates jury trials as the presumed constitutionally designed default mechanism rather than an anomalous “luxury.”

Countervailing Concerns Accepted by Reformers but Viewed as Solvable
• Sheer caseload: Trials consume 5–20× more resources. Reformers respond that scarcity forces efficiency: jurisdictions can (a) drop or divert low-level offenses, (b) raise charging standards, (c) add funding for courts, and (d) re-allocate prison money to judicial operations.
• Victim trauma and delay: Some defendants might seek delays to harass victims. Yet trials under speedy-trial rules neutralize indefinite extensions.

Illustrative Lines from Modern Abolitionist Literature
• “If the legislature cannot afford to give every defendant the jury trial promised in the Constitution, then it should repeal crimes, not coerce pleas.” (Albert W. Alschuler, 1979; reviving England’s 1970s Scarman critique).
• “Any system in which innocence is a plea-bargaining liability is indefensible.” (John H. Langbein, 2018 ABA speech).

Summary
Proponents argue that abolishing plea bargaining restores accuracy, curbs prosecutorial caprice, equalizes outcomes, and re-legitimizes the system. They concede the transition would be disruptive, but insist the short-term logistical shock is a price worth paying to align criminal justice with its founding constitutional and moral premises.

We stand at the gate of conscience.
Before it swings open onto the future of American justice, we must decide what— and who— will pass through.

I speak to you tonight not mainly as a lawyer, not as a policy analyst, but as a citizen whose heart still pounds when the word “freedom” is mentioned. In a nation that boasts the torch of liberty, we have allowed a shadow practice— plea bargaining— to strangle that torch until only embers remain. Tonight we declare: no more.

For decades we have been told that plea bargaining is a practical necessity. That without it, courts would collapse under their own weight. That without it, the guilty would go free and the innocent would languish even longer. These are not truths; these are alibis, hammered into place by fear and convenience. They are the rationalizations that every generation offers when it is too tired to do justice the hard way— the only way justice is ever done.

I ask you: if a system cannot survive unless it pressures the weak to surrender their constitutional right to trial— is it a justice system at all, or a ransom racket with robes?

Look into the numbers, because numbers have faces. Ninety-seven percent of federal convictions and ninety-four percent of state convictions never reach a courtroom. NINETY-FOUR PERCENT. That is not an efficiency statistic; that is the slow-motion burial of trial by jury. When the path to the courthouse is paved with coercion, innocence becomes just another bargaining chip. Black and Brown defendants— already over-policed— are handed offers they cannot refuse, frightened by the threat of sentences that multiply if they dare demand the trial the Constitution guarantees. Teenagers— scared kids— plead guilty to felonies they did not commit because a prosecutor whispers, “Take ten years now, or roll the dice on fifty.”

Tell me, where in the Sixth Amendment does it carve out a loophole labeled “practicality”? Where in the Fourteenth Amendment does it say, “Equal protection applies— unless the calendar is crowded”? Nowhere. Absolutely nowhere.

Those who defend plea bargaining claim it lightens penalties for the accused. They forget to add: only those who first confess— whether true or not. That is not leniency; that is a medieval ordeal repackaged in fluorescent lighting. It is a process that rewards exaggeration and punishes integrity, that turns public defenders into bean-counters, prosecutors into puppeteers, and judges— the very figures meant to stand above the fray— into clerks rubber-stamping “negotiated justice.” The result is not efficient; it is polluted.

Consider Kalief Browder— sixteen years old, accused of stealing a backpack, held at Rikers Island for three brutal years because he insisted on his innocence and would not plead out. The system broke his mind, then his body, then his life. Kalief did not die because we had too many trials. He died because we had too few.

We gather tonight to say: his fate must be the last casualty of this grotesque practice. We therefore call for the outright abolition of plea bargaining. Full stop. Every defendant— every single one— from the shoplifter to the CEO— gets an open trial with the evidence lit under constitutional daylight. Let DAs stop writing screenplays in charging documents, and start proving them. Let defense attorneys become defenders again, not just deal brokers. Let juries do what the founders bled to give them— judge facts and conscience side by side.

What will happen? The prophets of doom scream gridlock. I answer: justice delayed is less poisonous than justice denied. Let the states fund the courts they are required to run. Let outdated drug laws fall first, because they create the volume that destroys the docket. Let prosecutors triage their own consciences— “Do I believe this case so solid that I can swear to it before twelve citizens?” If not, don’t file it. Simple.

History is watching, and history doesn’t bargain. It records. It will record whether, at this hinge of the 21st century, we chose to trade human liberty for docket convenience. I refuse that bargain. I hope you refuse it too.

Imagine the America we can birth: parents teaching their children that if you are innocent, you can step into a courtroom without fear; that a public defender has the resources to match a DA; that a sentence is measured not by the hurry of the prosecutor, but by the gravity of the offense and the voice of the community manifested in a jury’s verdict; that the scales of justice stand free of the thumbprint of coercion.

To every lawmaker ready to tremble at the word “cost,” I say: calculate the cost of a ruined life, a lost generation, a republic that forgot its own promise. It dwarfs any budget line.

To every prosecutor who claims, “We can’t prove everything,” I say: then you shouldn’t charge everything. The burden of proof is the heartbeat of liberty. Tie it to your wrist, feel it pulse, and live by it— or trade your badge and your oath for a sales job.

We the People invented the trial on the principle that no power is so great it may not be questioned by ordinary citizens. If we discard that principle, we discard the mortar that holds the bricks of this republic together. The future we demand is simple: a courthouse door that opens, not a conveyor belt that spins.

The Case for Ending Plea Bargaining: Restoring Justice Through Full Trial

The American criminal justice system rests upon a foundation that seems simple in principle yet has become profoundly compromised in practice: the presumption that an individual is innocent until proven guilty, and that this determination should be made through a fair and public trial by an impartial jury. Yet this foundational promise has been systematically eroded by an institution that now handles the vast majority of criminal cases not through the adversarial process envisioned by the Constitution, but through backroom negotiations that sacrifice truth, fairness, and accountability on the altar of administrative convenience. Plea bargaining—the practice by which defendants plead guilty to reduced charges in exchange for more lenient sentences—has become the de facto method of case resolution, with some estimates suggesting that fewer than three percent of criminal cases actually proceed to trial. This represents not merely a statistical curiosity but a fundamental betrayal of the justice system's stated purpose. The time has come to abolish plea bargaining entirely and restore the trial as the primary mechanism for determining guilt and administering punishment.

The Coercive Foundation of Plea Bargaining

The most damning criticism of plea bargaining is that it operates through coercion rather than genuine choice. While prosecutors and defenders may describe plea agreements as "negotiations," this characterization obscures the profound power imbalance that defines these interactions. A defendant facing the prospect of decades in prison under charging enhancements, mandatory minimums, and habitual offender statutes is not entering a voluntary transaction; they are making a decision under extreme duress, one that any rational person in their position would feel compelled to accept regardless of their actual innocence or guilt.

This coercion falls heaviest upon those least equipped to resist it. A defendant who cannot afford bail sits in jail for months or years while awaiting trial, losing their job, their housing, their family connections, and their very sanity. For such individuals, accepting a plea deal that offers immediate release—however unjust the underlying charges—becomes the only viable option, even when they maintain their innocence. The Supreme Court itself has recognized that pre-trial detention creates "an almost irresistible pressure" to plead guilty, yet the Court has done little to address this fundamental injustice. The net result is a system in which liberty is traded for procedural regularity, and the threat of punishment becomes the instrument of punishment itself, imposed without the protections of trial.

The coercive dimension extends beyond the simple calculus of time served. Prosecutors wield the power to file additional charges, invoke sentencing enhancements, and invoke the specter of trial before a judge who may be perceived as hostile to the defendant's case. Defense attorneys, often overworked and under-resourced, may honestly believe that their client faces worse outcomes at trial and thus recommend acceptance of a plea deal. In this environment, the "choice" to plead guilty becomes less an exercise of free will than a forced submission to institutional pressure. The Constitution demands that guilt be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, not extracted through the threat of devastating punishment.

The Two-Tiered System of Justice

Plea bargaining has created a criminal justice system that operates differently for the wealthy than for the poor, transforming the principle of equality before the law into a cruel mockery. Those with substantial financial resources can afford private attorneys who have the time, experience, and relationships with prosecutors to negotiate favorable dispositions, or alternatively, to prepare robust defenses for trial. They can post bail and maintain their freedom while their case proceeds. They can afford expert witnesses, investigators, and the other resources that make effective defense possible. For these individuals, plea bargaining may indeed function as a genuine choice, an informed decision about how to resolve a legal matter.

For everyone else—the vast majority of defendants—plea bargaining operates as a mechanism of oppression. Public defenders, heroic though many of them are, carry crushing caseloads that make thorough investigation and zealous advocacy nearly impossible. A public defender in some jurisdictions may handle hundreds of cases simultaneously, leaving them with mere minutes to evaluate each file, consult with their client, and make critical decisions about trial readiness. In this context, the path of least resistance often leads to the recommendation that a client accept whatever deal the prosecutor is offering, regardless of the merits of the case. The systemic underfunding of public defense means that the state has effectively created a pipeline that funnels indigent defendants into guilty pleas, not because they are guilty, but because the system is designed to process them as efficiently as possible.

The racial dimensions of this two-tiered system compound its injustice. Studies consistently demonstrate that Black and Latino defendants face harsher charging decisions, receive less favorable plea offers, and receive longer sentences than similarly situated white defendants. Prosecutors exercise enormous discretion in deciding which charges to file and whether to offer plea agreements, and this discretion has been shown to be infected by implicit and explicit bias. A system that relies on plea bargaining is therefore a system that institutionalizes racial inequality, allowing the conscious and unconscious prejudices of individual prosecutors to determine outcomes without the corrective mechanism of public trial and judicial review.

The Erosion of the Presumption of Innocence

The presumption of innocence is not merely a legal technicality but the beating heart of criminal justice. It reflects a profound moral truth: that the power of the state against an individual citizen must be constrained by rigorous proof, and that it is far better for a guilty person to go free than for an innocent person to be punished. Yet plea bargaining fundamentally undermines this principle by treating the determination of guilt as a bargaining chip rather than a sacred fact to be established through adversarial process.

When a defendant accepts a plea deal, they are not admitting to facts that have been proven in court; they are acknowledging that the risks of trial outweigh the benefits of fighting charges. The question of actual guilt or innocence becomes secondary to the question of procedural strategy. This is not justice in any meaningful sense; it is a calculation of expediency that treats the finding of guilt as a commodity to be exchanged. The public never learns what happened in a particular case, because there is no trial to reveal the evidence, no cross-examination to test the prosecution's theories, no verdict to establish the truth. The community is denied its right to see justice done, and the defendant is denied the opportunity to clear their name through the process the Constitution guarantees.

The consequences of this erosion extend beyond individual cases to the health of the body politic. When most criminal cases are resolved through plea bargaining, the public loses faith in the criminal justice system's ability to discern truth. The spectacle of a trial—with its rules of evidence, its adversarial testing, its requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt—serves an educational function, demonstrating to the community that the state cannot simply accuse and condemn but must prove its case. Without this ritual, the criminal justice system becomes a black box, its operations inscrutable and its outcomes seemingly arbitrary. This breeds cynicism, distrust, and the dangerous perception that the system serves power rather than justice.

Innocent Defendants and the Tragedy of False Guilty Pleas

Perhaps the most horrifying consequence of plea bargaining is the certainty that innocent people have been wrongfully convicted through the process. While the American criminal justice system has developed mechanisms to exonerate the occasional convicted defendant through post-conviction DNA testing and innocence projects, these efforts have revealed only the tip of an iceberg of wrongful convictions. For every exoneree, there are countless others who accepted guilty pleas to crimes they did not commit, their innocence forever obscured by the bargain they made to avoid even worse punishment.

The phenomenon of innocent defendants pleading guilty is well-documented but inadequately understood. Research by Brandon Garrett and others has shown that many exonerees initially accepted guilty pleas before their convictions were overturned, often because they faced threats of much harsher punishment if they exercised their right to trial. In some cases, innocent defendants were coerced into pleas by overworked defense attorneys who believed their clients would be convicted anyway and wanted to spare them the risk of a death sentence or life imprisonment. In others, the psychological pressure of detention, the advice of counsel, and the fear of the unknown combined to produce decisions that haunt these individuals for the rest of their lives.

The problem is compounded by the fact that guilty pleas are essentially irrevocable. Once a defendant enters a plea, they have very limited grounds for appeal, and courts are extremely reluctant to overturn guilty pleas absent extraordinary circumstances. This means that the plea bargaining system creates a one-way ratchet: defendants who accept deals for crimes they did not commit have almost no recourse, while defendants who reject deals and are convicted at trial retain their appellate rights. The incentives are thus perverse, encouraging defendants to accept unjust deals to preserve some hope of eventual freedom, even when they are innocent.

The Corruption of Prosecutorial Power

Plea bargaining grants prosecutors virtually unchecked power over the outcome of criminal cases, and this power has proven susceptible to abuse. Prosecutors can determine, through their charging decisions, whether a defendant faces a modest misdemeanor or a decades-long felony. They can invoke sentencing enhancements that dramatically increase the mandatory minimums a defendant faces. They can threaten to file charges against a defendant's family members or associates, using the most vulnerable people in a defendant's life as leverage. And they can do all of this with minimal judicial oversight or public accountability.

This prosecutorial power is particularly dangerous because it operates in the shadows. Unlike trials, which are public proceedings subject to media scrutiny and judicial oversight, plea negotiations occur in private conferences where no record is made and no one observes the pressure that is brought to bear. A prosecutor who threatens a defendant with excessive charges in a public trial would be subject to criticism and possible judicial sanction; the same threat delivered in a plea conference is treated as legitimate negotiation. This asymmetry of transparency creates conditions in which prosecutorial overreach flourishes unchecked.

The institutional pressures that drive prosecutors to pursue plea bargains compound these concerns. Prosecutors are evaluated on their conviction rates and their ability to secure pleas, creating incentives to prioritize case clearance over justice. The sheer volume of criminal cases makes it administratively impossible to try them all, and so prosecutors areImplicitly encouraged to use the threat of trial to extract pleas. This is not to impugn the motives of individual prosecutors, many of whom enter public service seeking to serve their communities. Rather, it is to recognize that any system that rewards prosecutors for securing pleas will inevitably produce more pleas, regardless of the underlying merits of the cases involved.

The Misallocation of Resources

Proponents of plea bargaining often defend it as a necessary accommodation to limited judicial resources, arguing that trying every case would overwhelm the courts and produce unacceptable delays. This argument deserves scrutiny, because it presupposes that administrative convenience should take precedence over justice. We do not accept resource constraints as a justification for eliminating trials in civil cases or for dispensing with other procedural protections; we recognize that certain constitutional requirements are non-negotiable, regardless of cost.

Moreover, the resource argument rests on questionable empirical foundations. The explosion of plea bargaining has not reduced the workload of prosecutors, judges, and defense attorneys; it has simply shifted the nature of that work from courtroom advocacy to negotiation and paperwork. Courts have not become faster or more efficient; they have become sites of administrative processing where the appearance of justice substitutes for its substance. If resources are truly inadequate to conduct trials, then the appropriate response is to provide more resources, not to abandon the trial process altogether.

There is also a profound irony in the resource argument. The United States incarcerates more people per capita than any other nation in history, spending tens of billions of dollars annually on prisons and jails. The costs of this mass incarceration—in terms of destroyed families, communities, and human potential—far exceed the costs of conducting more trials. Yet plea bargaining is often defended as a cost-saving measure, even as it contributes to a system of over-incarceration that is economically unsustainable and morally indefensible. We are saving money on trials while spending fortunes on prisons, and we are told that this represents rational policy.

Restoring the Trial as the Heart of Criminal Justice

The alternative to plea bargaining is not chaos but restoration. If every criminal case were resolved through trial, we would need to rebuild our criminal justice infrastructure to handle this increased caseload. This would require more judges, more prosecutors, more public defenders, more courtrooms, and more support staff. It would require investment in jury management systems, evidence preservation, and all the other elements that make trials possible. It would be expensive, time-consuming, and disruptive.

But this investment would be worth it, because it would restore meaning to the promises embedded in our constitutional framework. Trials are not merely a means of determining guilt; they are a civic ritual that affirms the community's commitment to fairness, transparency, and the rule of law. When a jury of citizens hears the evidence and renders a verdict, they are not just deciding one defendant's fate; they are participating in a process that distinguishes our society from those where power operates unconstrained by law. The trial is the moment when the state must justify its accusation, when the defendant can confront their accusers, and when the public can see justice done.

Trials also serve as essential mechanisms for developing legal precedent and testing prosecutorial theories. Cases that go to trial produce appellate decisions that guide future conduct, clarify the boundaries of criminal liability, and check the power of prosecutors to stretch the law beyond its legitimate scope. Plea bargaining, by contrast, produces no precedent, no clarification, and no check. It is a dead end that consumes cases without contributing to the development of legal doctrine or the education of legal professionals.

Addressing the Objections

Critics of abolishing plea bargaining raise several objections that deserve serious consideration. First, they argue that defendants sometimes voluntarily choose to plead guilty because they are in fact guilty and wish to accept responsibility. This is true, but it misses the point. A defendant who is genuinely guilty and wishes to plead guilty can still do so; the question is whether such pleas should be encouraged and facilitated through the bargaining process, or whether they should be exceptional occurrences that happen only when the evidence is overwhelming and the defendant sees no viable defense. The current system incentivizes guilty pleas even when the evidence is weak; an abolition of plea bargaining would invert these incentives, making trial the default and guilty pleas the exception reserved for clear cases.

Second, critics argue that victims prefer plea bargains because they avoid the trauma of trial testimony. This concern is legitimate and deserves respect. However, victims should not be asked to sacrifice justice for their own convenience, and the desire to avoid difficult testimony should not be permitted to override the defendant's right to trial or the community's interest in knowing the truth. Moreover, many victims find closure in seeing their accuser face public accountability in a court of law; the trial process can be cathartic as well as traumatic. The criminal justice system should offer victims support and choice, but it should not structure its procedures around the assumption that trials are inherently harmful.

Third, critics argue that abolition would increase racial disparities by eliminating the one mechanism that sometimes produces lenient outcomes for disadvantaged defendants. This argument has surface plausibility, but it gets the analysis backwards. Plea bargaining produces lenient outcomes for some defendants while producing unjust outcomes for others; the very reason it produces leniency for some is that it enables harshness for others. The solution to unjust outcomes is not to expand the mechanism that produces them but to eliminate them. A system that requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt for every conviction would produce more just outcomes overall, even if it occasionally produces results that seem harsh in individual cases.

Conclusion

The case for abolishing plea bargaining is ultimately a case for taking our constitutional commitments seriously. The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury; the Fifth Amendment requires that no person be deprived of liberty without due process of law; the presumption of innocence is a foundational principle that traces back to the origins of Anglo-American jurisprudence. These guarantees mean nothing if they can be evaded through the simple expedient of threatening defendants with devastating punishment until they surrender their rights.

Plea bargaining has created a two-tiered justice system that punishes the poor and minorities more harshly than the wealthy and privileged. It has coerced innocent people into admitting crimes they did not commit. It has concentrated unreviewable power in the hands of prosecutors operating in secret. And it has eroded public confidence in the criminal justice system's ability to discern truth and deliver justice.

The path forward is not to reform plea bargaining but to end it. This will require sustained investment in court infrastructure, prosecutorial offices, and public defense. It will require political courage to face the short-term disruptions that accompany structural change. And it will require a recommitment to the principle that the state's power to deprive citizens of their liberty must be constrained by rigorous procedures designed to protect the innocent and punish the guilty.

This is a ambitious agenda, but it is not utopian. The American criminal justice system once tried far more cases than it does today, and it can do so again. The question is whether we have the will to restore the trial as the centerpiece of criminal justice, or whether we will continue to accept a system that trades efficiency for fairness and throughput for truth. The answer will define what kind of justice system we are, and what kind of society we aspire to become.

When plea bargains are common, sentencing becomes highly individualized based on bargaining dynamics rather than on the nature of the offense and the defendant's criminal history. A wealthy defendant with an excellent attorney may negotiate a far lighter sentence than a poor defendant with a public defender, even when the circumstances of their crimes are identical. Second, opacity prevents meaningful appellate review; if we do not know why a particular sentence was imposed, we cannot determine whether it was legally appropriate. Third, public confidence in the criminal justice system requires transparency, and a system where outcomes are determined by secret negotiations fails to provide the accountability that democratic governance requires.

A system without plea bargaining would base all sentences on publicly available information: the facts of the offense as established through evidence at trial, the defendant's criminal history, and applicable sentencing guidelines and laws. Judges would impose sentences in open court, with their reasoning visible to the parties, the public, and appellate courts. This transparency would promote consistency, enable meaningful appellate review, and restore public confidence in the fairness of the system.

Strengthening Prosecutorial Accountability

Prosecutors exercise enormous power in the criminal justice system, and plea bargaining concentrates this power while minimizing accountability. When prosecutors can secure convictions through negotiation without the work and uncertainty of trial, they face reduced pressure to build strong cases, evaluate evidence critically, or decline to prosecute when the evidence is weak. The ability to threaten severe sentences creates a leverage that often compels guilty pleas regardless of actual evidence quality.

Eliminating plea bargaining would fundamentally alter the calculus of prosecutorial decision-making. Prosecutors would know that every case they bring must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt in a public trial. This would encourage more rigorous initial evaluation of cases, greater care in evidence collection and preservation, and more willingness to decline prosecution when the evidence does not support conviction. The famous prosecutor's discretion to charge or not charge would be exercised with the knowledge that charging means committing to full trial.

This accountability would extend to the charging decisions themselves. Currently, prosecutors can file overly aggressive charges knowing that they can be reduced through negotiation, effectively using the charging power as a bargaining chip rather than as a reflection of the actual crimes committed. Without plea bargaining, prosecutors would need to charge what they can prove, knowing that the initial charging document largely determines the universe of possible convictions. This would encourage more accurate and proportionate charging from the outset.

Enhancing Deterrence and Respect for the Law

Paradoxically, the prevalence of plea bargaining may undermine the deterrent effect of criminal law. When most offenders negotiate their sentences down from the statutory maximum, the actual consequences of crime become disconnected from the potential consequences announced in statutes. The law on the books threatens severe punishment, but the law in practice delivers substantially less. This gap between threatened and actual consequences may reduce deterrence by communicating that the real-world costs of crime are lower than the stated costs.

A system without plea bargaining would align actual punishments more closely with statutory ranges. While judges would still exercise discretion within those ranges, the systematic reduction of sentences through negotiation would end. This would create greater certainty about the consequences of conviction— defendants would know that if they are found guilty, they will face the sentence the law provides rather than a negotiated reduction. Some research suggests that certainty of punishment matters as much as severity for deterrence, and eliminating plea bargaining would increase certainty by removing the expectation of routine reduction.

Beyond specific deterrence, the symbolic functions of criminal punishment matter for maintaining respect for the law. When the public perceives that plea bargaining allows wealthy or well-represented defendants to escape justice while ordinary defendants face the full weight of the law, confidence in the legal system erodes. A system where every case is determined by trial, where sentences are imposed transparently, and where the rules are applied consistently would strengthen public respect for the legal process and the law it enforces.

Promoting Judicial Efficiency and Resource Reallocation

While eliminating plea bargaining might seem to threaten court efficiency, a careful analysis suggests that it could ultimately promote more rational use of resources. Currently, the plea bargaining system consumes enormous resources in negotiation, motion practice, and preparation for cases that will never go to trial. Defense attorneys spend hours negotiating with prosecutors; prosecutors spend time evaluating offers and counteroffers; courts schedule status conferences and change of plea hearings. These resources are diverted from actual adjudication.

If plea bargaining were eliminated, the system would need to adapt. Some adaptations would involve short-term costs—hiring more judges, expanding court facilities, ensuring adequate representation for indigent defendants. But other adaptations would involve genuine efficiencies. Prosecutors would need to make faster decisions about whether cases are worth pursuing, reducing the time spent on marginal cases. Defense attorneys could focus on trial preparation rather than negotiation. Most importantly, the system would develop a clearer sense of its actual caseload, allowing for better long-term planning and resource allocation.

Furthermore, eliminating plea bargaining would reduce the current perverse incentives that the system creates. Currently, defense attorneys are sometimes incentivized to encourage clients to accept plea deals even when trial might be preferable, because trials require more work and generate more risk. Prosecutors may be incentivized to file excessive charges to create bargaining leverage. Judges may be incentivized to encourage pleas to manage caseloads. Removing plea bargaining would eliminate these distorting incentives and align the interests of all participants with the proper goal of accurate fact-finding.

Conclusion: Restoring the Promise of Criminal Justice

The case for eliminating plea bargaining rests ultimately on a vision of criminal justice that prioritizes fairness, transparency, and constitutional integrity over administrative convenience. This vision holds that the state should not deprive citizens of liberty without proving its case in public, that innocent people should not be coerced into confessions, that similar crimes should receive similar punishments, and that the operations of the criminal justice system should be visible and accountable to the public.

None of these principles is currently served by a system where more than nine out of ten cases are resolved through negotiation rather than adjudication. The plea bargaining system has become so normalized that it is often defended as inevitable, but its inevitability is a function of its own existence—once the system came to depend on plea bargaining to manage caseloads, the burdens of eliminating it seemed insurmountable. Yet the costs of maintaining this system are borne primarily by the defendants who are coerced into guilty pleas, the victims who are denied the closure of public trial, and the public which is denied the transparency and accountability that democratic governance requires.

A criminal justice system without plea bargaining would be a different system—one where the constitutional right to trial is real rather than theoretical, where innocence provides meaningful protection against conviction, where sentencing is consistent and transparent, and where prosecutorial power is checked by the requirement of proof. Such a system would require significant institutional adaptation and would undoubtedly face implementation challenges. But for those who believe that justice requires the state to prove its case, that liberty is too important to be surrendered under pressure, and that the public trial is the heart of criminal adjudication rather than an inconvenient relic, the elimination of plea bargaining represents not a utopian dream but a recovery of the system's founding commitments.

The Lament of the Plea Bargain Apologists: A Field Guide to Defending the Indefensible

Introduction: And They Say Crime Doesn't Pay

There is perhaps no group in American public life more tragically misunderstood than the devoted defenders of plea bargaining. These brave souls—who prefer to call themselves "criminal justice reform advocates," though reform in the direction of maintaining the status quo requires either a very flexible definition of both words—have been subjected to mockery, derision, and the occasional well-deserved eye-roll from anyone who has spent more than ten minutes thinking about how our legal system actually functions. And yet they soldier on, arguments at the ready, determined to explain why the practice of coercing defendants into waiving their constitutional rights is actually a cornerstone of justice, not a grotesque distortion of it.

What follows is an affectionate (and by "affectionate," I mean the opposite of that) tribute to the various strains of plea bargain apologism that greet anyone bold enough to suggest that, perhaps, forcing people to choose between exercising their right to a trial and facing catastrophic sentencing enhancements might not be the height of jurisprudential wisdom.

The Pragmatists: "But the Courts Will Collapse!"

First, we must address the "pragmatists," those clear-eyed realists who approach the question of plea bargaining not with moral reasoning but with the furrowed-brow concern of someone calculating whether they'll make it to their 3 PM tee time. The pragmatists have done the math, and their calculations show that without plea deals, the entire American justice system would transform into some kind of dystopian nightmare—presumably because judges would suddenly have to do their jobs.

According to these calculations, if every defendant exercised their constitutional right to a trial, courts would be overwhelmed. Prosecutors would be forced to actually prove their cases. Defense attorneys would have to, heaven forbid, provide adequate representation. The whole delicate machinery of mass incarceration would grind to a halt, and we would be left with the unpalatable necessity of either releasing people who haven't been proven guilty or actually investing in a justice system that can handle the volume of cases it processes.

The obvious response—that if the system cannot function without coercion, then the system itself is the problem—never seems to occur to the pragmatists. They view the plea bargain not as a bug in our justice system but as a feature, much as someone might view a seatbelt that also randomly shocks the driver as an acceptable compromise. "Yes," they seem to say, "the system is designed in such a way that it can only operate through threats and coercion, and our response to this revelation should be to maintain the threats and coercion rather than redesign the system."

One suspects that if the only way to keep restaurants running was to threaten customers with prison time if they didn't order quickly enough, the pragmatists would be at the forefront of the "Why Are You Trying to Destroy the Restaurant Industry?" brigade. The system is broken in a way that benefits certain outcomes, so therefore the brokenness must be preserved.

The Defense Attorneys: "I'm Protecting My Clients!"

Next, we turn to a truly impressive piece of cognitive dissonance: the criminal defense attorneys who defend plea bargaining as a necessary tool for protecting their clients. These well-meaning advocates have somehow convinced themselves that the practice of presenting a defendant with a choice between a guaranteed five-year sentence and a potential fifty-year sentence—with the trial date looming and the public defender's caseload hovering around three hundred active cases—is an act of zealous representation rather than an institutionalized shakedown.

The logic, such as it is, runs as follows: plea bargaining gives defendants "options." Without it, defendants would face the full fury of prosecutorial discretion without any means of mitigation. A good defense attorney can negotiate a better deal than the defendant would get after a trial, so therefore plea bargaining serves the client's interests.

This framing conveniently ignores the fundamental coercion at the heart of the system. A defendant isn't comparing a plea deal to a trial in any meaningful sense—they're comparing a known, manageable consequence to a potentially devastating one that could easily exceed any rational assessment of what the evidence might warrant. When the system stacks the deck so heavily against exercising constitutional rights that "choice" becomes a euphemism for "choose which finger you want smashed with a hammer," describing the resulting decision as a voluntary agreement borders on the absurd.

What's particularly amusing about this defense is how quickly it falls apart under scrutiny. If plea bargaining truly served defendants' interests, one might expect defendants to be enthusiastic participants rather than reluctant conscriptors. One might expect defense attorneys to advocate for maintaining the practice rather than reform that might reduce their caseloads and force them into the uncomfortable position of actually trying cases. One might expect the bar association to celebrate plea bargaining as a hallmark of American legal innovation rather than acknowledging, in hushed tones, that it's a necessary evil born of resource constraints and an insistence on processing unprecedented numbers of people through the criminal system.

But no. Instead, we get defense attorneys explaining that the crushing weight of the state's power, backed by mandatory minimums and sentencing guidelines that make any trial a high-stakes gamble, is actually a form of client protection. Next, they'll explain that working in a coal mine is actually great for cardiovascular health.

The Prosecutors: "Justice Requires Efficiency"

Perhaps no group has produced more creative rationalizations for plea bargaining than prosecutors, those dedicated public servants whose stated mission is to seek justice but whose performance metrics are based almost entirely on conviction rates. The prosecutor who opposes plea bargaining would be like a basketball coach who objected to keeping score—they might have some philosophical objections, but they're going to find themselves with a lot of time to contemplate those objections from the bench.

Prosecutors explain that plea bargaining is essential for "judicial efficiency," as if the purpose of a court is to process cases as quickly as possible rather than to determine guilt or innocence. They speak of "clearing dockets" and "conserving resources" with the same terminology one might use for clearing inventory or conserving office supplies, as though the product being moved isn't human freedom.

The efficiency argument has a certain surface-level appeal, in the way that any argument does when you don't think about it for more than two seconds. Our courts are overwhelmed! Our prosecutors are overworked! Without plea deals, justice would be delayed, and delayed justice is denied justice! All of this is technically true, in the same way that it's technically true that cutting off your leg would help you lose weight.

The missing piece of this analysis is the question of why the system is so overwhelmed in the first place. It isn't because Americans suddenly became more law-abiding and stopped committing crimes. It isn't because prosecutors are lazy or courts are inefficient. It's because we've constructed a system designed to arrest, charge, and convict unprecedented numbers of people, and then we're told that the only way to make this system run is to skip the tedious parts where we actually determine whether people are guilty.

The prosecutor who complains about being unable to handle a trial-heavy system is like a factory manager complaining that quality control inspections are slowing down production. The solution isn't to eliminate inspections—it's to recognize that the entire premise of the factory was flawed.

The "Reformers": "Go Slow, My Brother"

Then there are the incrementalists, those wise owls of criminal justice who recognize that plea bargaining has problems but insist that sudden reform would be disastrous. These careful stewards of change tell us that abolition is "too radical," that we need to "build consensus," that meaningful change requires "gradual implementation" over "realistic timelines."

The incrementalist approach to plea bargaining reform has a long and distinguished history of accomplishing absolutely nothing while feeling very responsible about itself. For decades, we've been told that we're not quite ready for fundamental change, that the conditions aren't right, that we need more study, more pilot programs, more committees, more reports. Each generation of incrementalists inherits the reforms its predecessors failed to accomplish and immediately relegates them to the status of "long-term goals" requiring further study.

What's particularly entertaining about the incrementalist position is how it maps onto virtually every injustice in American history. One can easily imagine the same arguments being deployed against abolition ("the economy isn't ready!"), against women's suffrage ("it would be too disruptive!"), against desegregation ("we must move at a pace the community can accept!"). The incrementalists are always patient, always reasonable, always certain that the perfect moment for justice is always somewhere in the future, conveniently never arriving.

The incrementalist's ideal reform timeline tends to look something like this: first, study the problem; then, create a task force; then, publish a report; then, implement a small pilot program; then, evaluate the pilot program; then, consider scaling up; then, face budget constraints; then, return to the study phase. Under this framework, plea bargaining will be abolished sometime around the heat death of the universe, which the incrementalists will no doubt describe as "a realistic timeline."

The Fiscal Conservatives: "Think of the Budget!"

Ah, the fiscal conservatives. These red-blooded defenders of limited government and fiscal responsibility have, when it comes to plea bargaining, discovered an issue they care about deeply. The same politicians who vant to cut social programs to the bone, who view any government spending as a moral failing, who tell us that we simply can't afford healthcare or education or housing—these same guardians of the public purse have suddenly discovered that the criminal justice system might be too expensive to maintain without plea deals.

It's a fascinating conversion experience. One moment, the fiscal conservative is telling us that we need to cut Medicaid because the budget simply can't support it. The next moment, they're explaining that we absolutely must maintain a system that coerces guilty pleas because trying cases would be too expensive. The math only works if you assume that the purpose of the criminal justice system is to spend as little as possible while locking up as many people as possible—which, actually, does describe the fiscal conservative's position fairly accurately.

What's especially charming about the fiscal argument against plea bargaining reform is how it reveals the underlying priorities. We're not concerned about wrongful convictions, or coercive pressure on the innocent, or the erosion of constitutional rights. No, those are abstract concerns. But the budget—now that's real. We can put a price tag on efficiency, and that price tag turns out to be more important than justice itself.

One imagines the same logic applied to other contexts: "Yes, we know that the hospital's policy of threatening patients with bankruptcy if they don't accept the cheapest treatment has some ethical issues, but have you considered how expensive it would be to actually treat people properly?"

The Victims' Rights Champions: "Think of the Victims!"

And finally, we come to the victims' rights advocates who oppose plea bargaining reform—not because they support the practice, mind you, but because they believe that abolition would somehow harm victims. These sincere and often passionate advocates tell us that victims have been "promised" closure through plea deals, that victims have made decisions based on the expectation of plea bargains, that victims need the certainty that plea bargaining provides.

This argument deserves more respect than it typically receives, because it does come from a genuine place of care for people who have suffered. The problem is that it manages to be both cynical and naive at the same time—cynical in how it uses victims as human shields for a practice that exists primarily to serve prosecutorial convenience, and naive in its assumption that the current system actually serves victims well.

The truth is that the plea bargaining system treats victims as afterthoughts, if it acknowledges them at all. Prosecutors offer plea deals without consulting victims. Victims show up to court expecting a trial and discover that a deal was cut weeks ago. The "closure" that plea bargaining supposedly provides often means watching the person who harmed you receive a sentence that both you and the prosecutor agreed was too lenient, with the explanation that it was the best that could be done under the circumstances. Victims are told to be grateful for whatever they get, because the alternative is the uncertainty of trial—and then they're blamed when they express dissatisfaction with the outcome.

The victims' rights argument against reform is the argument that victims need a system designed to coerce guilty pleas, because a system that required proof would somehow be worse for victims. This assumes that victims want convictions at any cost, that they don't care whether those convictions are earned through legitimate process, that certainty of outcome matters more than legitimacy of process. Most victims I've spoken to don't want someone punished just to feel better—they want the right person punished for the right reasons, which is rather difficult when that person was pressured into confessing to something they may not have done.

Conclusion: The Death of a Thousand Rationalizations

And so we arrive at the end of our tour through the landscape of plea bargain apologism, a journey through rationalizations so elaborate and so deeply held that one almost begins to suspect that the people making them believe their own arguments. Almost.

The common thread running through all these positions is a fundamental commitment to maintaining a system that can only function through coercion, combined with an unwillingness to acknowledge that commitment in honest terms. Everyone has a理由 for why the practice must continue, and those reasons all trace back to the same uncomfortable truth: we've built a machine for processing human beings that cannot operate without pressure, threats, and the systematic erosion of constitutional rights, and we'd rather maintain that machine than face the disruption of building something better.

The plea bargain apologists will continue to argue, to rationalize, and to explain why the unacceptable is actually necessary. And those of us who believe that a justice system that requires coercion to function isn't a justice system at all will continue to push for something better—not because we're naive about the challenges, but because we refuse to accept that the challenges are insurmountable simply because they're inconvenient.

In the end, the defense of plea bargaining comes down to a simple proposition: we cannot afford justice. The system is too big, the caseloads too heavy, the resources too limited. And so we must make do with something that merely looks like justice, acts like justice in some superficial respects, and provides most of the same outcomes—while sacrificing the essential ingredient that makes justice worth having.

The plea bargain apologists are wrong, but they're wrong in interesting ways that reveal deep truths about our values and our priorities. They're wrong because they've confused the map for the territory, the process for the purpose, the system's convenience for justice itself. And they're wrong in ways that will only become more apparent as the contradictions of our criminal justice system continue to unfold.

One day, we'll look back on the era of plea bargaining the way we now look back on other institutional shames—wondering how anyone could have defended it, questioning the moral clarity of our ancestors, grateful that we lived to see reform. The plea bargain apologists of today will be the opponents of obvious justice tomorrow, their arguments remembered mainly as cautionary tales about what happens when we mistake necessity for virtue.

Until that day, we'll continue to hear about the practical constraints, the resource limitations, the need for efficiency, and the importance of victim closure. And we'll continue to respond with the only answer that matters: if the system cannot function without coercion, then the system must change.

The Verdict We Owe: Ending Plea Bargaining and Restoring the Right to a Fair Trial

Mr. Chairman, distinguished members of this body, fellow citizens who believe in justice—I come before you today not as a legal scholar cloaked in abstract theory, but as a voice for every individual who has ever sat in a courtroom, terrified and alone, pressured to surrender their innocence not because they are guilty, but because the system has made the math of survival more terrifying than the math of truth.

I am here to demand an end to plea bargaining in America.

For decades, we have tolerated a practice that corrupts the foundations of our justice system. We have allowed prosecutors to become judges, for juries to become relics, and for the sacred constitutional right to a trial—the sixth amendment, the very heartbeat of American justice—to become a bargaining chip traded away in back rooms. We have built a machine that processes human lives through shortcuts, and we call it efficiency. I call it a disgrace.

The Coercion Hidden in "Choice"

Let me tell you what plea bargaining really is. It is a system that says to an accused person: "You can exercise your right to a trial and risk decades in prison, or you can admit guilt now and walk away with a lesser sentence." This is not justice. This is a gun to the head of liberty dressed up in legal language.

The word "choice" appears throughout our legal discussions of plea deals. But what choice exists when the alternative is a potential life sentence? What choice exists when a public defender, overwhelmed by 200 cases, advises their client that a trial is "too risky"? What choice exists when a mother of three, facing a prosecutor who wants to make an example of her, calculates that even a 10% chance of conviction means losing her children forever?

This is not choice. This is coercion wearing a suit and tie.

The numbers tell a damning story. In the federal system alone, over 97% of convictions result from guilty pleas. In state courts, the number exceeds 90% in virtually every jurisdiction. Ask yourself: are 97% of defendants actually guilty? Or have we built a system where admitting guilt becomes the rational option regardless of innocence?

The Innocent Who Plead

History provides the horrifying answer.

In 1984, a young man named Jeffrey Deskovic was convicted of a murder he did not commit. He spent fifteen years in prison for a crime DNA evidence later proved he did not commit. Why did he plead guilty? Because prosecutors offered him a deal: confess and receive a sentence that would make him eligible for parole in eight years. Fight it out at trial and risk a sentence that could keep him imprisoned for life. He chose what any rational person would choose when the odds are stacked against them. He chose survival over vindication.

The system broke Jeffrey Deskovic. It broke Paul Giannoni, who spent twenty-six years for murders he did not commit. It broke Keith Harshbarger, who lost fourteen years to a crime DNA proved he did not commit. Each of these men had something in common: they were pressured into plea deals, convinced that trial was too dangerous, that the system would never find them innocent after they had been accused.

How many others have we never heard about? How many innocent men and women, unable to take the risk of trial, have accepted guilt for crimes they did not commit? We cannot know the full scope of this injustice. But we know it exists, and we know it is not rare.

The Innocence Project has documented over 375 wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA evidence. A significant percentage of these individuals originally accepted plea deals rather than risk trial. If this is the toll among cases where DNA evidence eventually emerged to prove innocence, imagine the toll among the thousands of cases where no such evidence exists—where the innocent have quietly served their sentences, their names never cleared, their stories never told.

The Weight of Power

Plea bargaining does not simply risk injustice in individual cases. It fundamentally unbalances the scales of justice, concentrating terrifying power in the hands of prosecutors while stripping defendants of meaningful recourse.

When trial is the exception rather than the rule, prosecutors become the architects of criminal law rather than its servants. They decide who gets charged with what. They decide what evidence to present and what to withhold. They decide whether to offer mercy or to seek maximum punishment—not based on the facts of the case, but based on their assessment of whether a defendant will buckle under pressure.

This creates a two-tiered system of justice. Wealthy defendants with expensive lawyers can afford to go to trial. They can afford to exercise their constitutional rights. They can afford to make the state prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. But poor defendants—those who depend on overworked public defenders, who lack the resources to mount an aggressive defense—face a different reality. For them, trial is not a right to be exercised. It is a terrifying gamble that could result in a lifetime behind bars.

The result is a system that punishes the poor more harshly than the wealthy, that treats the constitutional rights of the wealthy as meaningful and the constitutional rights of the poor as theoretical. This is not justice. This is class warfare conducted through the machinery of law.

The Racial Dimension

We cannot discuss plea bargaining without confronting its racial dimensions. Study after study has documented that Black and Latino defendants receive harsher plea deals than white defendants charged with similar crimes. They are more likely to be charged under statutes that carry mandatory minimums. They are less likely to receive the benefit of prosecutorial discretion.

The Sentencing Project found that Black men are sentenced to terms that are, on average, 19% longer than those received by white men for comparable crimes. The War on Drugs has produced staggeringly disproportionate impacts, with Black Americans incarcerated for drug offenses at rates that far exceed their usage of drugs. Plea bargaining is the engine that drives these disparities deeper into the system, converting statistical unfairness into individual tragedy.

Consider the case of Cyntoia Brown, who was sentenced to life in prison for a murder she committed at age sixteen. She was offered a plea deal that would have resulted in her release after fifteen years. She rejected it. She chose to go to trial. She was convicted and received the life sentence. After serving fifteen years, she was granted clemency—not because the system recognized its error, but because public opinion finally demanded mercy.

Cyntoia Brown had the courage to exercise her right to trial. How many others, facing similar circumstances, have accepted plea deals that kept them locked away for decades for crimes that did not merit such punishment? How many have accepted deals not because they were guilty, but because the weight of the state's power crushed their will to resist?

The Myth of Efficiency

Defenders of plea bargaining argue that it is necessary—that our courts could not possibly handle the caseload if every case went to trial. They paint a picture of chaos, of clogged courts and delayed justice, of a system that would grind to a halt without the efficiency of plea deals.

I reject this framing entirely.

We do not build justice systems to be efficient. We build them to be just. The purpose of a court is not to process cases as quickly as possible. The purpose of a court is to determine the truth, to protect the innocent, and to punish the guilty according to law. If our courts cannot handle this workload, then we have built too few courts, hired too few judges, and allocated too few resources to the fundamental task of administering justice.

Imagine if we applied this logic elsewhere. Would we accept plea bargaining in medicine? "Rather than run the tests to diagnose your condition, doctor, why don't we just assume it's cancer and begin treatment? It would be so much more efficient." Would we accept plea bargaining in aviation? "Rather than thoroughly inspect this plane, let's just assume it's safe. The alternative would delay too many flights."

We would find such suggestions absurd. We would recognize that shortcuts in matters of life and death produce disasters. But in matters of liberty—matters where human beings can be locked away for decades, where families are destroyed and futures are stolen—we shrug our shoulders and call it pragmatism.

I call it a failure of leadership.

Restoring the Right to Trial

If we end plea bargaining, what happens next? Let me paint you a picture.

Courts expand to meet the need. We hire more judges. We fund more public defenders. We require prosecutors to actually prove their cases in open court, subject to cross-examination and public scrutiny. We return to the principle that a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that the burden of proof rests on the state.

This will require investment. It will require us to prioritize justice over efficiency, principle over convenience. But what is the alternative? A system where justice is reserved for those who can afford it? A system where the innocent plead guilty because the risks of trial are too great? A system where prosecutorial power knows no meaningful check?

I refuse to accept that America cannot afford justice. I refuse to believe that we are too poor, too busy, or too indifferent to provide every accused person with a real trial. We are the wealthiest nation in human history. We spend more on our military than the next ten countries combined. We can certainly afford a justice system that actually delivers justice.

The Constitutional Question

The sixth amendment to our Constitution guarantees the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury. It guarantees the right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation. It guarantees the right to confront witnesses against them. It guarantees the right to have compulsory process for obtaining witnesses in their favor. It guarantees the right to assistance of counsel.

Plea bargaining renders every one of these guarantees hollow. The trial becomes a theoretical option that is effectively unavailable. The right to confrontation is waived in exchange for a reduced sentence. The jury becomes a relic of an earlier age. The constitutional protections that were won through centuries of struggle— protections that distinguish American justice from the tyranny we fled—become empty formalities.

If we allow plea bargaining to persist, we are not merely tolerating a practical accommodation. We are surrendering the constitutional vision of justice itself. We are telling future generations that the rights enshrined in our founding documents are optional, negotiable, subject to the convenience of prosecutors and the budget constraints of state legislatures.

Is this the legacy we wish to leave?

A Vision for Justice

I believe in a different vision. I believe in a justice system where every accusation is tested. Where every defendant has their day in court. Every criminal case should be resolved through a full and fair trial because liberty must never depend on bargaining power, prosecutorial discretion, or fear of an extreme punishment.

The strongest objection to plea bargaining is that it undermines the presumption of innocence. In principle, an accused person is innocent until the government proves guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. This “trial penalty” turns the exercise of constitutional rights into a gamble. A defendant may face months in prison after a plea but decades if convicted at trial. Because most cases never reach trial, these decisions effectively determine outcomes. Judges and juries play only limited roles, while negotiations occur largely outside public view. The result is a system in which one party can shape both the accusation and the punishment without undergoing the full adversarial scrutiny that a trial provides.

This concentration of power increases the danger of arbitrary and unequal treatment. Two people accused of similar conduct may receive radically different outcomes depending on the prosecutor, jurisdiction, defense attorney, or willingness to plead quickly. Defendants who lack money, legal knowledge, or effective counsel are especially vulnerable. Pretrial detention can intensify the pressure: a person unable to afford release may plead guilty simply to leave jail sooner, even when a viable defense exists. Wealthier defendants, by contrast, may have the resources to investigate the case and resist coercive offers.
